name: Priya Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Lovely, I'm glad you asked. I've got the kettle on and the pigs are fed, so I've got an hour before the veg boxes need packing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day for you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a 90-acre smallholding from the county council, Brook End. Forty outdoor sows, a field of mixed veg, a few acres of oats, and a box scheme that goes to about 160 households every Thursday. I'm up at six, walk the pig paddocks, check the water troughs, then I sit down with my laptop and ask the AI to rework the week's picking list against what's actually ready. I chair the council tenants' association too, which is mostly unpaid meetings and arguing about drains.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you use AI for the picking list. How much do you use it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. Customer emails, pig records, rotation plans, even the newsletter. It's not magic, it gets things wrong, but it gives me back about two hours a day. Laszlo, my partner, is a carpenter and he thinks I've been taken over by a cult. The money's thin, though, no getting round it: the box scheme pays the rent and the feed and not much else, and we've about two weeks of cash in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a bit of a shame, actually. I'd post something on the growers' forum saying the tools are still useful, they just aren't going to save us. I'd say the real problems were always land prices and supermarket power anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means nothing changes for me, and that's not entirely good news. My problem is money, not machines. I was half hoping the robots would bring the cost of small-scale kit down so people like me could afford them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on using the AI for the admin and keep the box scheme growing, maybe to 200 households. I'd push the council for a longer tenancy, because a five-year lease is no way to plan anything. And I'd keep trying to put fifty a month aside, which I manage about half the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little disappointed, if that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why disappointed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've watched every new machine in farming get built for the 2,000-acre farm first and the little ones last. I'd hoped this time the clever stuff would be cheap enough for us. If it fizzles, the big ones keep their head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the 160 households notice, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, I hope. They'd get their Thursday box with a note from me and a recipe. The AI writes the recipe, I'll be honest, and I fix the quantities because it once told a family to use four kilos of chard.

S0.say: I'd say it's a bit of a shame, because the tools are useful even if they won't save us. I'd post on the growers' forum that the real problems were always land prices and supermarket power.
S0.think: I think nothing changes for me, and that's not all good. My problem is money, and I was hoping robots would make small-scale kit cheap enough for people like me.
S0.do: Carries on using AI for daily admin and aims to grow the box scheme to 200 households. Pushes the council for a longer tenancy and tries to save fifty a month.
S0.quote: The AI writes the recipe, I'll be honest, and I fix the quantities because it once told a family to use four kilos of chard.
S0.fieldNote: She is the rare farmer who'd be disappointed by a plateau, because she sees technology as a possible equaliser for small growers. Her pressure is money and tenancy length, not change itself. She speaks of AI as a flawed but useful daily helper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity, but only if the gains are shared. I'd say on the forum that small growers need public money to buy the kit together, or the big estates will hoover up all the benefits. I'd say workers on the big farms need retraining, not just a handshake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be quite excited. I'm among the best at what I do, but I'm one woman with forty sows and a bad shoulder. A robot that weeds my carrot beds overnight would be the best thing that's happened to Brook End.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the tenants' association to apply for a council grant for a shared robot weeder and a shared drone, kept in the old depot. I'd be first in the queue to trial it. And I'd learn the new pig-health software properly rather than poking at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a bit of nerves about the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You have about two weeks of cash. How would you pay for any of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't, not alone. That's the whole point of the shared kit, thirty tenants paying in a little each. If the council won't help, I'd try a crowdfunder from the box customers, they've backed me before when the barn roof went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lads who do the hand-weeding on the bigger farms over the hill. That's their summer wage gone. I'd want the robot money to fund jobs fixing and running the things, and I'd say so at every meeting.

S1.say: I'd say it's an opportunity only if the gains are shared, with public money helping small growers buy kit together. Workers on big farms need retraining, not just a handshake.
S1.think: I think I'd be quite excited, because I'm one woman with forty sows and a bad shoulder. A robot weeding my carrot beds overnight would be the best thing to happen to Brook End.
S1.do: Gets the tenants' association to apply for a council grant for a shared robot weeder and drone kept at the old depot, and volunteers to trial it first. Learns the new pig-health software properly and considers a crowdfunder from box customers.
S1.quote: I'm one woman with forty sows and a bad shoulder.
S1.fieldNote: She sees steady disruption as a chance for small growers if they club together, a strongly collective, progressive answer. Thin savings shape the plan: she can't buy alone, so she organises. Her concern for hand-weeding labourers was unprompted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency public ownership of the farm robots, or at least of the land, before the big money buys it all. I'd go to the council and the tenants' meetings and say council farms should be the test case for doing this fairly. I'd be loud about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me more than I'd admit. If AGI farms better and cheaper by 2028, supermarket veg drops in price, and my box scheme only survives if people still want a person behind it. At sixty, with two weeks' cash and a council lease, I'd be very exposed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd sit down with Laszlo and cut everything that isn't feed or rent. I'd turn the box scheme into more of a membership, farm days, cooking with the kids, things people pay for because a person is there. I'd use the AI to help write a proposal to the council for a tenant-run robot co-op.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Busy anxious, though, not frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having just two years change, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can't wait for the council, they take two years to fix a gate. With two years I'd have to do it with the tenants and the customers and whatever I can scrape together. With more time I could do it properly, with grants and a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned farm days. What would one look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Saturday morning, ten families, bacon sandwiches. The kids feed the sows, we pull carrots, I tell them how the soil works. A robot can grow a carrot, but it can't make a nine-year-old care about one.

S2.say: I'd say we need public ownership of farm robots or the land before big money buys it all. Council farms should be the test case for doing it fairly, and I'd be loud about it online.
S2.think: I think it scares me more than I'd admit, because cheap robot-grown veg could undercut my box scheme. At sixty, with two weeks' cash and a council lease, I'd be very exposed.
S2.do: Cuts everything except feed and rent with her partner in the first month. Turns the box scheme into a membership with paid farm days and uses AI to draft a proposal for a tenant-run robot co-op.
S2.feel: Anxious, but busy rather than frozen.
S2.quote: A robot can grow a carrot, but it can't make a nine-year-old care about one.
S2.fieldNote: Even here she reaches for organising and reinventing, not retreating. Her private fear centres on prices falling under her box scheme. She was clear that two years rules out waiting for the council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do it right, so let's see councils and the government back small farms to share the kit. I'd say the gains from AGI should pay for land reform. I'd say it at every meeting I could get to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I think I'd actually do well. I'd be the tenant who learned it first and helped the others, and that's worth something. I'd be 63, still fit enough, with the robots doing the heavy lifting my shoulder can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd get the shared kit co-op set up and trial a robot on my own veg beds. I'd start the farm days as a second income in spring. And I'd use the time to get a ten-year lease out of the council, which is the thing that would let me plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the edges, mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a contradiction between wanting public ownership and wanting to do well yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I want everyone to do well, I just know I'll be at the front of the queue because I enjoy this stuff. If the co-op works, the tenant next door who hates computers gets the same robot I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years give you that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lease, mostly. With two years I'm scrambling. With five, I can argue the council into a ten-year tenancy and build something that outlasts my shoulder.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to do it right, with councils and government backing small farms to share kit. The gains from AGI should help pay for land reform.
S3.think: I think I'd actually do well, as the tenant who learned it first and helped the others. At 63 the robots would do the heavy lifting my shoulder can't.
S3.do: Sets up a shared kit co-op and trials a robot on her own veg beds in the first year. Starts paid farm days as a second income and uses the time to win a ten-year council lease.
S3.feel: Mostly hopeful, uneasy at the edges.
S3.quote: If the co-op works, the tenant next door who hates computers gets the same robot I do.
S3.fieldNote: Five years shifts her from scrambling to building. She sees her own early adoption as a public good rather than a personal edge. The lease length keeps coming back as her real constraint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to make this good for everyone, so no excuses. I'd say every small farm should get a robot and every farm worker should get a share of what it earns. I'd say it on the forum, at the council, and at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, ten years feels manageable, even good. I'd be 68, the robots would be cheap by then, and I could hand Brook End to a younger tenant with the kit already working. The money would still be thin, but less of my body would be in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put what little I can into shares in the tenants' co-op, so I own a slice of the kit, not just rent it. I'd automate the weeding and the pig water first, the jobs that wreck me. And I'd campaign for council farms to stay as starter farms for young people, robots or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mira works in software, so she'd tell me I'm being naive. Dani would want to come home and run it with me. I'd tell them both the land's not ours, it's the council's, and that's fine as long as the council keeps it for people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You have very little saved. Does that not worry you over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a bit. But I'd rather own a share of a robot than a share in a bank that pays me nothing. If the co-op works, that's my pension, sort of.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to make it good for everyone, with a robot for every small farm and a share of the earnings for every worker. I'd say it on the forum, at the council and at the pub.
S4.think: I think ten years feels manageable, even good, with cheap robots by then and Brook End handed on with the kit working. The money would still be thin, but less of my body would be in it.
S4.do: Puts what she can into shares in the tenants' co-op so she owns part of the kit. Automates weeding and pig watering first and campaigns for council farms to stay as starter farms for young people.
S4.quote: I'd rather own a share of a robot than a share in a bank that pays me nothing.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she is close to optimistic, despite having almost no savings. She treats co-op shares as a kind of pension, which is hopeful but untested. Her plan always comes back to collective ownership.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to organise. What would help is public money and land security for small farms, a long lease and a share in the machines, so people like me aren't just pushed out by whoever can buy a robot first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about food. If robots make cheap food, brilliant, nobody should go hungry. But I'd like there to still be a farm where a kid can stand in the mud and see where it comes from. That's worth paying a person for.

headlineQuote: I'd like there to still be a farm where a kid can stand in the mud and see where it comes from.
portrait: Priya Varga is 58 and rents a 90-acre council smallholding with outdoor pigs, veg and a box scheme, earning little and keeping about two weeks of cash. She uses AI every day for admin and chairs the tenants' association. Strongly progressive, she sees AI and robots as a chance for small growers if they own the kit together, and she'd be first to try it. Her worry peaks with AGI in two years, when there's no time to organise, and eases into hope with a decade to prepare.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there would be no time to organise tenants and cheap robot-grown food could undercut her box scheme.
whatWouldHelp: Public money and land security for small farms: a long lease and a share in the machines, so they aren't pushed out by whoever buys a robot first.
